newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine unions strike over Menem's job "betrayal".
newsitem.headline: Argentine unions strike over Menem's job "betrayal".

text.p: Argentine unions began a 36-hour general strike on Thursday accusing President Carlos Menem of betraying workers and the Peronist labour movement and robbing the country of job security.

Tens of thousands thronged Buenos Aires' Plaza de Mayo to hear the head of the main CGT union federation, Rodolfo Daer, warn the Peronist government that "it cannot rule with its back to the people and the people will not forgive betrayal."

The CGT had been an ally of Menem since he came to power in 1989, but called a "Strike And A Half" in protest at 17.1 percent unemployment, labour reforms in favour of employers and recent tax hikes and worker benefit reductions.

The stoppage that began at noon (1500 GMT) is the second in two months. Menem complained this week that the labour unrest would cost the economy $2.7 billion -- or one percent of gross national product. Flights were disrupted and financial markets had what one trader called a "wasted day" of slow business. Public transport chaos was expected on Friday.
Menem angered unions and opposition parties by calling it a "tourist strike" -- an excuse for a long weekend.
But Daer, once a Menem confidant, snapped back in a speech to a crowd he estimated at 100,000 people: "We are here to say that they are the tourists and we are the working men."

It looked like the strongest challenge yet to Menem's free-market economic reforms, which have been hailed for reducing inflation to zero from 5,000 percent since he took power but which have also doubled unemployment.

Menem and Economy Minister Roque Fernandez stood defiantly by their reforms. Menem wrote in La Nacion newspaper "Strikes don't stop laws" and Fernandez told reporters: "No way are we thinking of changing the economic plan."

Flushed with success after Congress finally approved his tax austerity package -- fuel and income tax hikes designed to plug a growing budget deficit -- late on Wednesday, Fernandez said: "No way are we thinking of changing the economic plan."

Underscoring his determination to chase fiscal solvency rather than job-creation, Fernandez announced the sell-off of the state mortgage bank Banco Hipotecario, valued at $3-3.5 billion, and added that public transport fares may go up.

Menem vowed to push ahead with labour reforms to lower employers' costs and make them more likely to take on staff. He wants wages dependent on economic conditions, looser rules on working hours and holidays, collective pay deals scrapped and redundancy payments replaced by unemployment insurance.
"They want to destabilise unemployment but we will not let them," said Daer.

Opposition Radical Party leader Rodolfo Terragno said the strike showed "Menem's margin to continue with policies that have produced monstrous unemployment, recession and social discontent is narrowing."

In the historic Plaza, the sun, drums, peanut vendors, blue-and-white flags and portraits of Peronist Party founders Juan and Evita Peron gave the protest a festive air; but the message for Menem was anything but friendly.

As the crowds struck up the "Peronist March", the head of a CGT delegation from Concordia in Entre Rios province moaned that his city "was one of the most prosperous in the country before this corrupt government came. Now it has one of the highest levels of unemployment in Argentina."
